title: Characterizing the Edge of Stability in Variational Training Without Priors
claim: Using fewer Monte Carlo samples in variational training yields flatter minima and smoother functions, which improves out-of-distribution generalization.
layout: 3 toy-fit panels, then sharpness curve and OOD bar; left-to-right, dashed threshold line
description: The figure has two parts. Panel (a) is three small square plots titled M = 1, M = 5 and M = 100. Each shows a gray polynomial curve fitted through three black data points. The curve gets wigglier as M grows, and the annotated norm ||f|| rises from 0.86 to 1.2 to 1.7. The caption below reads 'Sharpness ≥ 1 + 2||f||'. Panel (b) is a line plot of sharpness against epoch. A blue line for standard training and an orange line for variational training each have a shaded band around them. A dashed gray horizontal line marks the 2/learning-rate threshold at 200. The blue curve reaches or crosses the threshold, while the orange stays below it. To the right, a partly visible OOD-accuracy panel (y-axis about 0.72–0.74) shows blue error bars. The eye goes first to the colored curves in (b).
caption: Variational training with fewer parameter samples leads to better generalization. The number of parameter samples used to estimate the expected loss in variational training (without prior regularization) affects the sharpness of the minima at convergence. A smaller number of samples \( M \) leads to convergence to flatter minima, which correspond to more regular functions (see (a); c.f. [ref]), thus explaining the observed improved generalization. In (b), we show the sharpness of the loss during standard and variational training of a ResNet on CIFAR-10. Notably, in the variational case the sharpness remains below the standard threshold of \(2 / learning rate\). When evaluated on a test set with distribution-shift, the variational model generalizes better out-of-distribution.
abstract: Variational approaches in deep learning promise to deliver improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution generalization by inferring a distribution over weights, regularized by a divergence to a chosen prior. However, prior elicitation presents a significant challenge in deep learning, resulting in the common practice of significantly downweighting the regularization term in the variational objective. Recently, it was proposed to train solely via the expected loss by relying on implicit regularization from the optimizer, rather than explicit regularization from the divergence to the prior. While this approach largely sidesteps the issue of prior elicitation, current theory lacks an understanding of how key optimization hyperparameters impact the implicit regularization. Here, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima of the loss landscape, which are known to generalize better. We show that training on the expected loss operates at a modified edge of stability, characterized by the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmark datasets confirm the practical significance of the theoretical results.
